section.title: The Prince of Tyre and Against Sidon
section.sectionRationale: This chapter closes the Tyre sequence with two oracles, one against the ruler of Tyre for claiming to be a god, and a second lament for the king of Tyre cast in imagery of Eden and a guardian cherub, before turning briefly to judge neighboring Sidon and closing with a promise of Israel's secure return to her own land.
section.thesis: Human pride that claims divine status, however wise or wealthy it becomes, will be humbled to the dust by the God who alone is truly exalted, while His own scattered people will one day be gathered home to dwell securely, free from every hostile neighbor.
section.frameNote: Four movements: judgment on the ruler of Tyre for claiming to be a god; a lament over the king of Tyre using imagery of Eden and a guardian cherub cast down; a shorter oracle against Sidon; and the promise that Israel will dwell securely in her own land.

units.label: The ruler of Tyre judged
units.note: I am a god, you are but a man

verses.text: And the word of the LORD came to me, saying,

“Son of man, tell the ruler of Tyre that this is what the Lord GOD says: Your heart is proud, and you have said, 'I am a god; I sit in the seat of gods in the heart of the sea.' Yet you are a man and not a god, though you have regarded your heart as that of a god.
Behold, you are wiser than Daniel; no secret is hidden from you!
By your wisdom and understanding you have gained your wealth and amassed gold and silver for your treasuries.
By your great skill in trading you have increased your wealth, but your heart has grown proud because of it.
Therefore this is what the Lord GOD says: Because you regard your heart as the heart of a god,
behold, I will bring foreigners against you, the most ruthless of nations. They will draw their swords against the beauty of your wisdom and will defile your splendor.
They will bring you down to the {{bor|Pit}}, and you will die a violent death in the heart of the seas.
Will you still say, 'I am a god,' in the presence of those who slay you? You will be only a man, not a god, in the hands of those who wound you.
You will die the death of the uncircumcised at the hands of foreigners. For I have spoken, declares the Lord GOD.”

units.label: A lament for the king of Tyre
units.note: in Eden, a guardian cherub, cast down

verses.text: Again the word of the LORD came to me, saying,
“Son of man, take up a lament for the king of Tyre and tell him that this is what the Lord GOD says: 'You were the seal of {{tokniyt|perfection}}, full of wisdom and perfect in beauty.

You were in Eden, the garden of God. Every kind of precious stone adorned you: ruby, topaz, and diamond, beryl, onyx, and jasper, sapphire, turquoise, and emerald. Your mountings and settings were crafted in gold, prepared on the day of your creation.
You were anointed as a guardian {{keruv|cherub}}, for I had ordained you. You were on the holy mountain of God; you walked among the fiery stones.
From the day you were created you were blameless in your ways, until wickedness was found in you.
By the vastness of your trade, you were filled with violence, and you sinned. So I drove you in disgrace from the mountain of God, and I banished you, O guardian cherub, from among the fiery stones.
Your heart grew proud of your beauty; you corrupted your wisdom because of your splendor; so I cast you to the earth; I made you a spectacle before kings.

By the multitude of your iniquities and the dishonesty of your trading you have profaned your sanctuaries. So I made fire come from within you, and it consumed you. I reduced you to ashes on the ground in the eyes of all who saw you.
All the nations who know you are appalled over you. You have come to a horrible end and will be no more.'”
Then the word of the LORD came to me, saying,
“Son of man, set your face against Sidon and prophesy against her.

And you are to declare that this is what the Lord GOD says: 'Behold, I am against you, O Sidon, and I will be glorified within you. They will know that I am the LORD when I execute judgments against her and demonstrate My holiness through her.
I will send a plague against her and shed blood in her streets; the slain will fall within her, while the sword is against her on every side. Then they will know that I am the LORD.
For the people of Israel will no longer face a pricking brier or a painful thorn from all around them who treat them with contempt. Then they will know that I am the Lord GOD.'

units.label: Israel gathered in security
units.note: the LORD shown holy among them

verses.text: This is what the Lord GOD says: 'When I gather the house of Israel from the peoples among whom they have been scattered, I will show Myself holy among them in the sight of the nations. Then they will dwell in their own land, which I have given to My servant Jacob.

And there they will dwell securely, build houses, and plant vineyards. They will dwell securely when I execute judgments against all those around them who treat them with contempt. Then they will know that I am the LORD their God.'”

bor.gloss: The Pit, a term for the grave or the realm of the dead. The proud ruler who claimed to sit 'in the seat of gods' is brought down to this lowest of destinations, a deliberate irony between his claimed height and his actual end.

tokniyt.gloss: A pattern, measure, or perfection, here rendered 'seal of perfection.' The term describes something measured out completely, whole and lacking nothing, a description that, applied to a creature rather than the Creator, becomes the very seedbed of pride.

keruv.gloss: A cherub, an exalted angelic being elsewhere pictured guarding Eden's entrance and the ark of the covenant. Whether this title describes the human king of Tyre in extravagant royal metaphor or points through him to a heavenly being fallen through pride is genuinely debated, and this passage is read carefully with that honest uncertainty.

basic.context: This chapter completes the three chapter sequence on Tyre with two closely related oracles: a plain judgment on Tyre's ruler for claiming divine status because of his wisdom and wealth, and then a lament for 'the king of Tyre' cast in extraordinary imagery, Eden, precious stones, and a guardian cherub, before turning briefly to a shorter oracle against neighboring Sidon and closing with a hopeful promise that Israel will one day dwell securely in her own land.
basic.hermeneutics: The first oracle, against the ruler or prince of Tyre, verses 1 to 10, clearly describes a proud human king judged for claiming to be a god. The second passage, the lament for the king of Tyre, verses 11 to 19, uses language so exalted, Eden, the garden of God, a guardian cherub, the holy mountain, that faithful readers have long debated whether it describes the human king alone in poetic hyperbole or uses him as a lens onto a greater fallen being behind human pride. This passage holds both readings with appropriate humility rather than forcing a single conclusion.
basic.originalLanguages: The king is called a keruv, a cherub, an exalted term used elsewhere for the beings who guard Eden and the ark, applied here either as royal metaphor or as a genuine glimpse of a heavenly power behind human pride. He is called the seal of tokniyth, perfection or completeness, a description properly belonging to God alone. And his end is the bor, the Pit, the lowest possible destination for one who claimed the highest possible seat.
basic.typology: The garden of Eden, the holy mountain, and the guardian cherub cast down for pride form a rich typological backdrop echoing Genesis 3's fall and anticipating the final judgment of every proud power, whether human or spiritual, before the God who alone remains exalted forever.
basic.christ: Where the king of Tyre corrupted his wisdom because of his splendor and was cast down from the mountain of God, Christ, though truly divine, did not grasp at equality with God but humbled Himself, and was for that humility exalted to the highest place, Philippians 2:5-11, the perfect reversal of Tyre's proud self exaltation and fall.
basic.god: God alone is truly exalted; every claim to divine status made by a creature, however wise, wealthy, or beautiful, will be shown false and humbled to dust. Yet the chapter does not end in mere judgment; it closes with God's tender promise to gather His scattered people home to dwell securely, showing that His holiness is displayed not only in judging pride but in keeping covenant love.
basic.crossReferences: Genesis 3:1-24 gives the pattern of pride, a garden, and a serpent figure cast down that this lament clearly echoes. Isaiah 14:12-15 gives a strikingly similar lament over the king of Babylon, long read alongside this passage as together hinting at a fallen heavenly power behind proud human rulers. Philippians 2:5-11 contrasts Tyre's self exaltation with Christ's humility and consequent exaltation. Revelation 21:1-4 answers this chapter's Eden imagery with the final restoration of God dwelling securely with His people.
basic.oneStory: Human pride that claims to sit in God's own seat is always, finally, humbled to the Pit, however wise or beautiful it appears; yet God's greater purpose is not mere judgment but gathering His scattered people home to dwell securely with Him, a promise fulfilled and secured forever in Christ, who alone was truly exalted because He first humbled Himself.

context.literary:
Chapter 28 contains three separate speeches, and the shift between them is the key to reading it. The first, verses 1 to 10, is addressed to the 'ruler' of Tyre, in Hebrew a nagid, a leader or prince. The second, verses 11 to 19, is a lament, a qinah, for the 'king' of Tyre, a melek. The third, verses 20 to 24, turns to Sidon, and verses 25 and 26 close with a promise to Israel. The change from ruler to king, and from a plain oracle to a lament, signals that the second speech works at a higher pitch than the first.

The first speech is built as a lawsuit with a clear charge and sentence. Verses 2 to 5 are the accusation, which turns on the word 'heart', 'Your heart is proud', 'you have regarded your heart as that of a god', 'your heart has grown proud'. The verdict begins with 'therefore' in verse 6 and is stated in terms of what the ruler claimed, so the god who says 'I am a god' will meet his killers 'in the heart of the seas' and be shown to be 'only a man'. The ending 'For I have spoken' gives the verdict a seal.

The second speech is different in kind. It is poetic and personal, and it moves like a story with a beginning, a rise and a fall: created, adorned, appointed, blameless, then found wicked, driven out, cast down, burned. The movement is tight. Each stage of the king's splendour in verses 12 to 14 is answered by a stage of his disgrace in verses 16 to 19. The adornment of verse 13 is stripped, the cherub's place on the holy mountain is lost in verse 16, and the fire of verse 18 reduces him to ashes.

The Sidon oracle is brief and contains no stated charge, and Ezekiel concludes the cycle of seven nations' oracles with a note about Israel, an unusual pairing that brings the section into line with the larger book. The whole series closes with a promise that makes it a message of hope for the exiles.
context.historical:
The 'ruler' of verse 2 is Tyre's reigning king in the years after Jerusalem's fall. Tyre was a city-state whose rulers held power through trade, naval strength and sacral standing. Its great god was Melqart, a name that means 'king of the city', and a Phoenician king would have presented himself as the god's earthly steward. So the claim of verse 2, 'I sit in the seat of gods', fits a political culture in which sacred and royal prestige overlapped. Behind the boast lay a real island fortress, 'in the heart of the sea', that no army had taken.

Wisdom was a Phoenician reputation. Tyre was famous for skilled craftsmen and cunning traders, and 1 Kings 5:6 to 10 shows King Hiram's workers and counsel serving Solomon. The sneer 'you are wiser than Daniel' in verse 3 is therefore both a recognition and a taunt. Daniel, a young exile in Babylon who was already known for insight, is named alongside Noah and Job in Ezekiel 14:14. To say Tyre's king thinks himself wiser is to say he thinks himself the equal of the greatest known wise men.

Eden and gemstones would also have had meaning to Tyre's neighbours. Every stone in the list of verse 13, in the BSB's rendering, appears among the twelve on the high priest's breastpiece in Exodus 28:17 to 20, with only jacinth, agate and amethyst absent. A BSB footnote says the identification of some of the stones is uncertain. Genesis 2:12 says gold and onyx are found in the land of Eden. The picture is of a garden-sanctuary, richly adorned, in which the king served.

Sidon, the older Phoenician city, lay north of Tyre. It is named in the table of nations as Canaan's firstborn, Genesis 10:15, and was the home of Ethbaal, whose daughter Jezebel married Ahab and brought Baal worship into Israel, 1 Kings 16:31. The 'pricking brier' of verse 24 describes Phoenician and Canaanite neighbours, long a thorn to Israel, as Numbers 33:55 had foretold of the nations left in the land.
context.canonical:
Ezekiel 28 is the centre of a web of texts about pride and a fall from a height. Genesis 3 is the basic one: a garden, a prohibition, a creature who wants more, and an expulsion from the place of God's presence with a cherub stationed on the east side, Genesis 3:24. Ezekiel 28:13 to 16 takes the Eden story as its template. The king is 'in Eden, the garden of God', walks 'among the fiery stones', is driven out 'from the mountain of God', and the cherub 'banished'.

Ezekiel himself uses the Eden pattern for others. Pharaoh is a great cedar in the garden of God, Ezekiel 31:8 to 9, whose pride leads to his being cast down 'to the depths of the earth to be with the trees of Eden', Ezekiel 31:16 to 18. Eden is Ezekiel's way of describing the highest height a ruler can reach, and the fall from it is a fall from the sacred centre of the world.

Isaiah 14:12 to 15 is the closest parallel. There the king of Babylon says, 'I will ascend to the heavens' and 'I will make myself like the Most High', and is brought down 'to the lowest depths of the Pit'. Both passages take a human tyrant as their immediate subject and use language of heaven. Readers have long set them side by side.

In the New Testament, Jesus says, 'I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven', Luke 10:18, and Paul warns that a recent convert could 'fall under the same condemnation as the devil', 1 Timothy 3:6, which assumes that the devil's sin was pride. Second Thessalonians 2:4 pictures a man who seats himself in God's temple, 'proclaiming himself to be God', the same boast as Ezekiel 28:2. In Acts 12:21 to 23, Herod, speaking to the people of Tyre and Sidon, is hailed as a god and struck down 'because Herod did not give glory to God'. Revelation 21:19 to 20 returns to the jewels, adorning the foundations of the new city.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Ezekiel's task here was to show the exiles that the pride of kings is a spiritual matter before it is a political one. The ruler of Tyre did not simply win wealth by skill; he came to believe that skill made him divine. The charge in verse 2 sets 'I am a god' beside 'you are a man', and Ezekiel wants his hearers to feel the gap. A man who sits at the heart of the sea and says he is a god is at the mercy of a stranger's sword.

The more elaborate lament in verses 11 to 19 had a second aim. The exiles had grown up on stories of Eden, the holy mountain and the cherubim, because those were the shapes of their own temple. Ezekiel takes this sacred vocabulary and says that anyone who stood in such a place and was given such gifts, and who then turned the gifts into self-worship, was cast out. This is a warning to the Israelite hearers as well. They had been 'in the garden of God', in a sense, in a land and a temple, and they too had been driven out.

The oracle against Sidon and the promise to Israel at the end hold the whole chapter together. The exiles are not left with only a tale of falling. They are told that their neighbours will no longer be a 'pricking brier', and that the LORD will gather them and show Himself holy among them. Pride's fall is the background; the gathering is the foreground.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter describes judgment on a proud ruler and city and a divine intention to restore Israel. It does not tell us how to identify the powers behind modern leaders, and it should not be used to build a detailed account of how and when a heavenly being fell. Careful readers will not say more than the text allows.

What the passage does teach by example is clear. Pride that takes the gifts of God, wisdom, wealth, beauty, and treats them as one's own is the oldest sin. It shows how achievement can turn the heart, since the king's wisdom brought wealth and the wealth made him proud, verses 4 and 5. It exposes the particular danger of dishonest trade, verse 18, which corrupts holy things.

It also gives believers a pattern for hope. The same prophet who foresaw a fallen king saw a gathered people. The promise of verses 25 and 26 is not a command but a divine commitment, and it invites trust rather than action. We are to live as people who expect to be gathered, not as people who must secure themselves, which is the opposite of the ruler's way in verse 2.

debates.question: Does the lament over the king of Tyre, verses 11 to 19, describe only a proud human king in extravagant poetic language, or does it also picture the fall of Satan behind that human pride?

views.label: A hyperbolic lament describing a proud human king alone
views.case: Ancient Near Eastern royal ideology commonly described kings in exalted, even semi divine language, comparing them to Eden or the gods; read this way, the whole lament, garden, cherub, fiery stones, is extravagant court poetry applied to Tyre's actual, historical ruler, whose trade made him wealthy and whose wealth made him proud, exactly as the preceding oracle in verses 1 to 10 plainly states about the same figure. Ezekiel also uses Eden for Pharaoh, Ezekiel 31:8 to 18, and the word 'created' is used of the Ammonites' origin in Ezekiel 21:30, so neither detail forces a heavenly reading.

views.label: The human king's fall pictures, or is overlaid with, the fall of a heavenly being, traditionally identified with Satan
views.case: Details that stretch beyond any human king, being anointed as a cherub, walking among the fiery stones, being blameless from creation until wickedness was found, closely parallel language many readers connect to Isaiah 14's similarly exalted lament over the king of Babylon and to later Jewish and Christian traditions about an angelic fall through pride; on this reading the human king becomes a kind of window onto the greater spiritual pride and fall that stands behind and inspires human tyranny. Early Christian writers such as Origen and Tertullian read the passage this way.

views.label: The king is cast as a new Adam, whose story repeats the first man's failure
views.case: The garden, the gold and onyx of Genesis 2:12, the walking in the garden, the status as 'blameless' until wickedness is found, and the expulsion east of Eden all follow the Genesis story closely. On this reading the lament compares the king to the first human, set in a sanctuary garden with a priestly role, who failed and was driven out. The cherub language reflects the guardian role given to Adam in Genesis 2:15 and the cherubim posted afterward, Genesis 3:24.

debates.bearing: Because faithful, careful readers genuinely disagree here, and because Scripture itself does not settle the question explicitly in this text, the views are presented with humility; either way, the passage's clear moral center holds, that pride which claims what belongs to God alone will be brought down, whether the immediate reference is a human king, a fallen spiritual power, or both together.

debates.question: Which Daniel is meant by 'you are wiser than Daniel' in verse 3?

views.label: Daniel the exile in Babylon
views.case: Ezekiel 14:14 lists Noah, Daniel and Job together as men of righteousness, and the book of Daniel presents a young Judean taken in the first deportation who was given understanding in every kind of wisdom. He was a contemporary of Ezekiel, famous among the exiles, and the irony of a proud king of Tyre who thinks himself wiser would be sharp for those hearers.

views.label: A legendary wise man of older tradition
views.case: Some scholars note that Ezekiel's spelling of the name differs from the one in the book of Daniel and point to a legendary wise judge in the Canaanite literature of Ugarit. On this view Ezekiel's reference is to a figure the Phoenician audience would know, which would give the taunt more bite, since it measures the king against their own proverbial sage.

debates.bearing: The text does not stop to explain, and the passage's point does not depend on the answer. Whether Daniel is a Judean exile or a figure of Canaanite tradition, the verse is irony: the king believes that nothing is hidden from him, and he is told he is only a man.

study.originalLanguages:
The first verse worth noticing is the claim of verse 2, 'I am a god', in Hebrew el ani, and the phrase for the seat, mosheb elohim, 'seat of gods'. The ruler is told in the same verse that he is 'a man', adam, and 'not a god', el. The Bible uses the same contrast whenever a creature overreaches. Isaiah 31:3 says of Egypt, 'the Egyptians are men, not God', and Hosea 11:9 has the LORD say, 'I am God and not man'. The ruler is made to say what Scripture elsewhere says only of God.

Next, verse 2 and verse 8 repeat 'heart of the seas', the phrase Ezekiel 27 used to mark Tyre's pride and wreck. Together with the repeated 'heart' of pride in verses 2 and 5, the effect is a pun in the poet's own idiom: a city that thinks its heart is divine meets death in the heart of the sea.

The wisdom vocabulary, chokmah, marks the whole chapter. It is the ruler's boast in verses 3 to 5, the 'beauty of your wisdom' that foreign swords will defile in verse 7, the king's fullness in verse 12 and what he 'corrupted' in verse 17. The same word carries both the achievement and the fall. The corresponding word for trade, rekullah, appears in verses 5, 16 and 18, and it too has a three-stage story: trade by which wealth is gained, trade that fills with violence, and trade that is dishonest. 'Violence', chamas, in verse 16 is the very word used of the earth before the flood, Genesis 6:11.

In verse 13 and 15 the verb for 'created', bara, is the same verb that opens Genesis. Careful readers do not need to force a heavenly meaning from it, because Ezekiel 21:30 uses the verb of the Ammonites in the place where they 'were created', their homeland. The verb says that the king was made and given his station, and it denies him self-origination. The word for 'blameless', tamim, is used for Noah in Genesis 6:9, and the verb 'walked' in verse 14 is the same stem used of the LORD walking in the garden, Genesis 3:8.

The phrase translated 'guardian cherub' in verse 14 is, in Hebrew, a cherub described by a word often rendered 'covering' or 'guardian'. Cherubim in the temple 'overshadow' the mercy seat, Exodus 25:20, and the picture is of a being in direct service of the divine presence.

Finally, the 'seal of perfection' in verse 12 is difficult. A seal marks a finished work, and the second noun is the word tokhnit, which can mean a measured pattern or plan. Translators have chosen different words for it. The sense is that the king was presented as the finished model of a ruler.

Verse 22 has 'I will be glorified' and 'demonstrate My holiness', and verse 25 has 'I will show Myself holy'. The holiness verb, from the root qadash, is the same in verses 22 and 25, and it is used for what the LORD shows through judging Sidon and through gathering Israel.

typology.type: Eden, the garden of God, as a type of the sanctuary, Ezekiel 28:13-14
typology.fulfillment: Ezekiel describes the garden as a mountain sanctuary adorned with stones and guarded by a cherub, a picture continued in Israel's tabernacle and temple, with cherubim on the veil and the mercy seat, Exodus 25:20 and 26:31. In Christ the sanctuary is fulfilled in a person, who says of His body, 'Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up again', John 2:19, and in the new Jerusalem, whose foundations are adorned with every kind of precious stone, Revelation 21:19. The correspondence is that the stones return, but in a city where nothing unclean enters. The type falls short as the king's Eden is a lost place, and the new one is permanent.

typology.type: The proud ruler who claims a god's seat, Ezekiel 28:2
typology.fulfillment: The ruler of Tyre claims divine status and is told he is only a man. The pattern recurs in Herod, who sits on his throne when the people of Tyre and Sidon seek peace and is greeted, 'This is the voice of a god, not a man', and is struck down, Acts 12:21 to 23. It reaches its highest point in the 'man of lawlessness' of 2 Thessalonians 2:4, who seats himself in God's temple 'proclaiming himself to be God'. In Christ the pattern is reversed, since the one who truly is God took the form of a servant, Philippians 2:6 to 8. The type falls short in that none of these figures is the final enemy by himself.

typology.type: The king cast down from the mountain of God, Ezekiel 28:16-17
typology.fulfillment: The king is thrown to the earth and made a spectacle. In the gospels, Jesus announces a corresponding judgment on the ruler of this world, 'the prince of this world will be cast out', John 12:31, and says of His disciples' mission, 'I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven', Luke 10:18. The escalation is that this is not a spectacle for kings but a defeat achieved through the cross. The correspondence is real only if Ezekiel's lament has a heavenly background, and since that is debated, the New Testament links are better read as parallels of theme than as proof that Ezekiel 28 describes Satan.

typology.type: Israel gathered to dwell securely, Ezekiel 28:25-26
typology.fulfillment: The promise to gather the house of Israel from the peoples and plant them in security anticipates the shepherd-king of Ezekiel 34:25 to 28 and the one flock of John 10:16, in which Jesus gathers other sheep who are not of this fold. In Christ the gathering reaches beyond Israel, since He gathers 'the scattered children of God', John 11:52. The type falls short in that Ezekiel pictures a land, while the New Testament sees a people gathered to a person, and a kingdom that is finally the new creation.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ by contrast, by the way the New Testament uses its themes, and by its closing promise.

The contrast is the clearest. The king of Tyre 'regarded your heart as that of a god' while being a man. Christ, who is truly God, 'did not consider equality with God something to be grasped, but emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant', Philippians 2:6 to 7. Where the king rose by wisdom and fell by pride, Christ descended by humility and was raised to the highest place, Philippians 2:8 to 9. The Gospels confirm that He did not trade on His status. In the wilderness He refused the offer of every kingdom of the world at the price of worship, Matthew 4:8 to 10.

The wisdom contrast is equally sharp. Tyre's ruler is told 'no secret is hidden from you', verse 3, and he used the claim to exalt himself. Of Christ it is said that 'in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge', Colossians 2:3, and Paul calls Him 'the power of God and the wisdom of God', 1 Corinthians 1:24. The true wisdom is not a possession that inflates its owner but a gift in a person who serves.

Third, the language of Eden and the holy mountain meets its fulfilment in Christ. He is the one who restores what the king lost. Ezekiel 28:13 puts the king in Eden, and Revelation 22:1 to 2 returns to the river and the tree of life through Christ, the Lamb.

Fourth, the promise of verses 25 and 26 points to Christ the gatherer. The LORD says, 'I will gather the house of Israel', and the good shepherd says, 'I have other sheep that are not of this fold; I must bring them also', John 10:16. The holiness the LORD shows through judging Sidon and gathering Israel is displayed finally at the cross, where judgment and mercy meet.

A word of care is needed. Whether Ezekiel 28 refers directly to Satan is disputed, and it is not a prophecy of Christ. The links above do not depend on settling that question. They rest on the way the New Testament picks up pride, exaltation, humility and gathering, and sets Christ as the answer to each.
study.god:
The chapter shows a God who alone is God. The ruler of Tyre says, 'I am a god', and the LORD answers with the simplest statement in Scripture, 'you are a man and not a god'. All the wisdom, wealth and beauty of Tyre are real but created, and creation does not become the Creator. The oracle is a sharp expression of the first commandment, that no one stands in the place of God.

He is the giver of wisdom, wealth and beauty. The king is told that he was 'full of wisdom and perfect in beauty', and that these things were 'prepared on the day of your creation'. What the king took as his own was given. The chapter shows a God who gives generously, who adorns with every precious stone, who appoints and ordains, and who gives so freely that a creature might forget the Giver. His gifts are not a trap, but they can be misused.

He is holy in a way that is displayed. The word 'holy' runs through the chapter: the holy mountain, the sanctuaries profaned, and the LORD's pledge to 'demonstrate My holiness' through Sidon and 'show Myself holy' among Israel. Holiness is not hidden in God's inner life. It is shown in the world, in the judgment of pride and the gathering of a people, and both are the one holiness.

He is just and measured. The sentences follow the shape of the offences. A king who claimed to be a god dies a violent death at human hands. A king whose trade filled him with violence is consumed by fire from within. The judgment comes both from outside, in the foreigners of verse 7, and from inside, in verse 18, where the fire comes from the king's own midst. Sin is its own destroyer under God's hand.

He keeps covenant. The chapter ends with the pledge that Israel will dwell securely in the land given to 'My servant Jacob'. The same God who casts down a proud king keeps His promise to a scattered people. The reason is not Israel's merit but His own name, as Ezekiel 36:22 will say. The refrain of verse 26, 'the LORD their God', is the covenant form of the recognition formula.

For worship, the chapter teaches us to receive wisdom, wealth and beauty as gifts, and to answer them with thanks rather than boasting. It calls us to humility before the one God, and to trust the God who gathers.

crossReferences.note: Cherubim are stationed on the east side of Eden to guard the way to the tree of life. Ezekiel 28:14 and 16 uses a cherub in the garden and says he was banished from the mountain of God. The two texts share the cherub, the garden and the expulsion, and the lament is built on the Genesis frame.

The king of Babylon says, 'I will make myself like the Most High', and is brought down to the Pit. Together with Ezekiel 28, it forms the pair of laments where a tyrant's pride is expressed in the language of heaven. Whether they describe only the human kings or also a spiritual power is the debate readers have long carried between them.

Egypt is described as a great tree in the garden of God, the envy of all the trees of Eden. Ezekiel uses the Eden setting here for a human monarch, which shows that the garden language of chapter 28 may be Ezekiel's way of describing the highest height of any ruler.

The LORD tells the Ammonites that He will judge them 'in the place where you were created'. The verb for created in Ezekiel 28:13 and 15 is used here of a nation's origin, which shows that the word does not need to mean the creation of an angel.

Herod, in dispute with the people of Tyre and Sidon, is hailed as 'the voice of a god, not a man' and is struck down because he did not give glory to God. It is the New Testament's neat echo of Ezekiel 28:2, set in the same two cities.

The LORD says, 'I am God and not man.' This is the mirror image of Ezekiel 28:2 and 9. What the king claims, God states truthfully, and the contrast of 'God' and 'man' is the oldest way the prophets expose pride.

The nations left in the land would become 'barbs in your eyes and thorns in your sides'. The 'pricking brier' of Ezekiel 28:24 uses the same picture, and shows that the old warning has come true. The oracle promises the end of the thorn.

Christ, in the form of God, did not grasp at equality with God but humbled Himself, and God exalted Him. It is the perfect reverse of Ezekiel 28:2 and 17, where a man grasps at divinity and is cast down.

All the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden in Christ. Against the ruler of Tyre who thinks no secret is hidden from him, Ezekiel 28:3, Paul sets the one in whom real wisdom is stored, and who uses it for service rather than self-exaltation.

The foundations of the new Jerusalem are adorned with every kind of precious stone, many of them the same kinds named in Ezekiel 28:13. The jewels of the lost garden return in the city where God dwells with His people, and are no longer a ground for pride.

study.oneStory:
The Bible begins in a garden, with a sanctuary, a gift and a warning, and Ezekiel 28 is one of the places where that beginning is retold. The lament over the king of Tyre uses Eden as its template: the garden of God, the holy mountain, stones and gold, a cherub, a blameless creature, and then a fall. Whatever else it means, it reminds readers that the oldest story of pride is not an isolated tale but the pattern for every later one.

The chapter answers a recurring question from Genesis. If humanity was made to rule under God, why do human rulers so often claim to be gods? The answer is that the temptation of Genesis 3, 'you will be like God', never goes away. It reappears at Babel, in Pharaoh, in the king of Babylon, in the ruler of Tyre, in Herod and in the man of lawlessness. Each time the claim is met with the same reminder, 'you are a man and not a god'.

The chapter also sets up what follows. Ezekiel's nation oracles end with Egypt, and then the book turns to hope. The final verses of this chapter, with the end of the brier and the gathering of Israel, hand over to the shepherd chapters, Ezekiel 34, and to the promise of a new covenant and a new heart, Ezekiel 36 and 37. The sentence on the proud and the promise to the humble belong to one message.

The story comes to rest in Christ. The first Adam was placed in a garden and failed. The Son who is the true image, Colossians 1:15, humbled Himself and was exalted, Philippians 2:8 to 9. He defeats the one who exalted himself, and the New Testament says the ruler of this world is cast out, John 12:31. The tyrant of every age falls with that fall.

The new creation brings Eden back with its jewels, its river and its tree, Revelation 21:19 to 22:2, but without the serpent and without a thief. There is no more curse, and God's people see His face. In that city no one says 'I am a god', for every voice says that the Lamb is worthy, Revelation 5:12, and Israel and the nations dwell securely in the presence of the God who gathered them.

quiz.q: What specific claim did the ruler of Tyre make that provoked judgment in verses 1 to 10?

options.text: He said, 'I am a god; I sit in the seat of gods in the heart of the sea.'
options.note: Verse 2 quotes this exact claim as the provoking sin.

options.text: He refused to pay taxes to Babylon.
options.note: Not mentioned in this passage; the stated sin is his claim to divine status.

options.text: He built an idol temple in Jerusalem.
options.note: Not described here; the accusation concerns his own self deification, not idol building elsewhere.

options.text: He was simply wealthier than any other ancient king.
options.note: Wealth itself is mentioned, verses 4 to 5, but the specific provoking sin is his claim to be a god, not wealth alone.

quiz.q: What imagery does the lament over the king of Tyre, verses 11 to 19, use to describe him?

options.text: He was in Eden, the garden of God, anointed as a guardian cherub, walking among the fiery stones.
options.note: Verses 13 to 14 use exactly this exalted imagery.

options.text: He is compared to a common shepherd tending sheep.
options.note: The imagery used is Eden and a guardian cherub, not shepherding language.

options.text: He is compared to a soldier defending a border fortress.
options.note: The passage's imagery is cosmic and Edenic, not military fortress language.

options.text: He is compared to a merchant selling goods in a marketplace.
options.note: Trade is mentioned as the source of his pride, verse 16, but the central imagery of the lament itself is Eden and cherub language.

quiz.q: How does this passage handle the debate over whether the lament describes only a human king or also pictures a fallen spiritual power?

options.text: It presents both readings honestly, since faithful interpreters genuinely disagree and Scripture does not explicitly settle the question in this text.
options.note: This reflects a careful, humble approach consistent with how the debate is framed for this passage.

options.text: It insists dogmatically that the passage is only ever about Satan and never about a human king.
options.note: This overstates certainty the text itself does not provide; the preceding oracle, verses 1 to 10, plainly addresses a human ruler.

options.text: It insists dogmatically that the passage could never refer to anything beyond an ordinary human king.
options.note: This dismisses a long, serious interpretive tradition too quickly; the imagery genuinely exceeds ordinary royal description.

options.text: It claims the debate has no bearing on the passage's moral meaning at all.
options.note: The debate does not change the clear moral center, that pride which claims what belongs to God is humbled, but it is not irrelevant to how the passage is read.

quiz.q: What is Sidon judged for in verses 20 to 24?

options.text: The LORD announces He will be glorified and shown holy by executing judgments against her, ending her role as a painful thorn to Israel.
options.note: Verses 22 to 24 tie Sidon's judgment to God's glory and to removing a lasting source of contempt against Israel.

options.text: Sidon is judged for a specific act of gloating over Jerusalem's fall, exactly like Tyre.
options.note: Unlike the earlier Tyre and Ammon oracles, no specific gloating quote from Sidon is recorded here; the emphasis is on God's glory being shown through judgment.

options.text: Sidon is condemned for claiming to be a god, exactly like the ruler of Tyre.
options.note: That specific claim belongs to the ruler of Tyre, verse 2, not to Sidon in this shorter oracle.

options.text: Sidon is condemned solely for economic rivalry with Tyre.
options.note: The text does not describe rivalry with Tyre as the reason; it centers on God's glory and holiness being displayed through judgment.

quiz.q: How does the chapter conclude, in verses 25 to 26?

options.text: With a promise that Israel will be gathered from the nations to dwell securely in her own land, building houses and planting vineyards.
options.note: Verses 25 to 26 explicitly promise this secure gathering and settled life for Israel.

options.text: With a warning that Israel will face renewed judgment before Sidon does.
options.note: The passage's tone here shifts to hope and promise for Israel, not further warning against her.

options.text: With a final oracle against Egypt introduced immediately.
options.note: The Egypt oracles begin in the next chapter, 29, not within this chapter's closing verses.

options.text: With an unresolved question about Israel's future left open.
options.note: The passage closes with a clear, positive promise, not an unresolved or open ended question.

questions: The ruler of Tyre let his wisdom and wealth convince him he was like a god. What success or ability in your own life tempts you to feel unaccountable to God?

The king of Tyre is described as blameless 'until wickedness was found' in him, corrupted by his own beauty and trade. Where has something genuinely good in your life quietly become a source of pride rather than gratitude?

This passage holds two views on the king of Tyre's lament with honesty rather than forcing one answer. Where else in your walk with God do you need to hold a hard question with humility rather than pretending to certainty you don't have?

Christ, unlike the king of Tyre, did not grasp at equality with God but humbled Himself, and was exalted as a result. Where is God inviting you to choose humility this week rather than self exaltation?

The chapter ends with Israel gathered to dwell securely, no longer surrounded by hostile neighbors. What would it look like for you to live today out of the security of that promised future rather than out of anxiety about present threats?

translationNotes.note: The Hebrew distinguishes 'ruler' (nagid) in the first oracle, verses 1 to 10, from 'king' (melek) in the lament, verses 11 to 19; most interpreters take both titles as referring to the same office or figure, though the shift in title has fed the debate over whether the lament reaches beyond the human ruler alone.
The precise identification of some of the nine listed gemstones is uncertain in Hebrew and varies between translations; the general sense of complete, priceless adornment is not affected.

The phrase 'guardian cherub' translates language whose exact grammatical force is debated among Hebrew scholars, some reading it as 'with an anointed guardian cherub I placed you' rather than identifying the king himself as the cherub; this uncertainty is part of why the passage is read with interpretive humility.
